extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readership (U.S. public and policymakers)
extracted.subtask_description: A multi-article front/section of a wartime American newspaper covering military actions, government policy disputes, press-access controversies, labor-board decisions, and human-interest casualty/POW reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press access and transparency (correspondents' principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The American people 'are entitled to know the decisions made through prompt, on-the-ground reporting by their traditionally free press.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Washington correspondents protested a reported exclusion of reporters from an international food conference, arguing that barring newsmen would be 'an abridgment of the freedom of the press' and would deny the public news they are entitled to and prevent public influence on decisions. The executive argument for exclusion was that the meetings 'will deal with military matters' and should be 'executive' to avoid hampering efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: OWI domestic-operations policy: facts over promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: OWI policy guide: 'We deal in one plain commodity — the facts the people of this country need to win the war. ... All the facts must be presented accurately and in proper proportion. Emotional appeals ... are not applicable to war problems.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OWI's stated duty is to supply information about fundamental war issues, problems that demand attention and cooperation, and things people must do to help themselves and the nation. The office says it is 'content to be judged by our output.' This is offered as the guiding standard for war-information operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid promotional 'slick salesmanship' in wartime information
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics (resigning OWI staff) asserted that 'activities of OWI on the home front are now dominated by high-pressure promoters who prefer slick salesmanship to honest information.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While promotional techniques have a legitimate function, the resigners argued they are inappropriate for war problems; the public deserves truthful, proportioned facts rather than emotional appeals or slogans. They cited misleading statements to the public and Congress as a reason for their resignations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely release of internal reports (OWI example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resigning staff complained that important internal reports (e.g., a food report prepared in January) were not released and ought to have been.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit standard: important informational reports relevant to public welfare and wartime planning should be released promptly; failure to do so undermines transparency and fuels internal disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: WRA release wage requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: War Relocation Authority (WRA) requirements call for paying the prevailing wage where the work is performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary Ickes stated that wage arrangements for released internees met standard WRA requirements (prevailing local wage). He also noted releases followed customary background investigation procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for release of internees to civilian work
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases of Japanese internees for civilian employment follow investigations by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and Military Intelligence and must meet WRA wage and other procedural standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ickes negotiated releases citing humanitarian reasons and labor needs; he referenced FBI/Military Intelligence vetting and compliance with WRA wage rules as prerequisites for release.

rubrics_metrics.name: War Labor Board / AFL principle: respect the tripartite process
rubrics_metrics.description: AFL members argued the President's executive order conflicted with the tri-partite War Labor Board process agreed with the President and that future cases should not be settled contrary to that agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AFL contended that changing the rules (via executive order) would cause injustices upon American labor and industry, weaken the board's effectiveness, erode worker confidence, and penalize workers for WLB delays—in short, decisions on wages and disputes should follow the agreed tripartite procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wage-increase policy restraint under executive order
rubrics_metrics.description: The President's order forbade general wage increases except under the Little Steel formula; the board trimmed a recommended wage increase and refused raises for correction of inequalities on the ground that the Executive order prohibited it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes a standard limiting wage adjustments during wartime unless they meet narrowly defined formulas; labor leaders criticized the blanket restriction as unfair to tens of thousands of workers and inconsistent with previous agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators/factors likely to produce wartime inflation (British economic assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: British experts: 'All the conditions that make for inflation are present in Germany.' Bombing destroys consumer goods and production means, disrupts transport, upsets manpower, and does not destroy an equivalent amount of purchasing power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors — destruction of goods/production capacity, transport disruptions, manpower losses, unequal impact on purchasing power — will likely speed inflation and foster black markets. Historical German countermeasures (looting occupied territories, price fixing, forced savings, using forced labor) are noted but seen as running out of effectiveness; morale and economic controls affect inflation dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military campaign planning: coordinated land-and-air assault principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Secretary of War Stimson forecast a 'coordinated Allied land and air assault' to climax the North African campaign, with the Eighth Army making the major attack and American Second Corps performing holding attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This articulates an operational principle: use coordinated land and air power, allocate holding and main-attack roles among allied forces, preserve mastery of the air, and prepare for substantial enemy resistance if they choose to fight rather than evacuate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naval shipbuilding policy: retain Navy construction authority
rubrics_metrics.description: House Naval Committee: proposal that the Navy stop building a type of auxiliary ship and let the Maritime Commission alone build them 'at this time would be catastrophic' and would make the Navy 'a pensioner' of the War Shipping Administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee recommended building 1,000,000 tons of new vessels and urged that Congress preserve Navy authority to build auxiliaries so the Navy's needs can be met 'in an orderly manner' rather than ceding control to another agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training standard for aircrew gunners: comprehensive, meticulous training
rubrics_metrics.description: The air force concluded that 'making a man a gunner and nothing else is too costly' and described meticulous training for air-to-air fire including practical turret control and sighting practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gunners require thorough, realistic training (ground firing, turret manipulation, sighting, trained in conditions resembling actual combat) and should not be limited to narrowly defined roles without broader crewmember competencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of casualty/POW notifications and next-of-kin procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: The War Department issued lists of personnel held prisoners and casualties reported to next of kin (including names, ranks, and relatives' contact information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard practice in reporting wartime casualties/POWs includes formal departmental lists and notification to next of kin with identifying details; accuracy and timeliness are implied standards for such communications.
